explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. David says it plainly: "From the ends of the earth I call out to You whenever my heart is faint." He calls out when his heart is faint, and he says so out loud. That's the part I love.

Nope, friend, and I get why it's tempting. The text says David calls out "…whenever my heart is faint." A proud heart doesn't usually go looking for a rock to be led to. David's heart is worn out, and he says so out loud.

Glad is a nice word, friend, but it's not the one in the psalm. David says he calls out "…whenever my heart is faint." I think a faint heart is a tired one. Notice what he does with it: he doesn't hide it, he takes it straight to God.

explanations.answer: To the rock higher than himself
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David prays, "Lead me to the rock that is higher than I." Think about that one. He's not saying he'll climb up there on his own. He asks to be LED, and I can relate, because I couldn't get out of that junk drawer by myself either.

Good guess for a king, baker, but the psalm never mentions a palace. David says, "Lead me to the rock that is higher than I." The place he asks for is a rock, and it's higher than he is. Nobody has to hang curtains up there.

explanations.answer: To his father's house in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: Home is a fine thought, friend, but a father's house isn't in this psalm. David asks, "Lead me to the rock that is higher than I." He's asking for a rock that's higher than he is, not a trip back to a house. And again, he asks to be led.
Right on, baker. David says, "For You have been my refuge, a tower of strength against the enemy." Look at the words "have been." He's talking about what God has been to him, and that's a refuge.

A teacher is a good thing to have, friend, but that's not what David says here. The verse says God has been his "…refuge, a tower of strength against the enemy." When an enemy is coming, you don't need a lecture. You need a place to run, and that's what a refuge is.
Not this time, baker. David calls God his "…refuge, a tower of strength against the enemy." He doesn't call Him judge here. A tower of strength is a pretty good thing to have against an enemy.
Yes, baker! David prays, "Let me dwell in Your tent forever…" Not a quick stop, a forever stay. Believe me, after years stuck in the back of a junk drawer, I know a good forever when I hear one.
One night is a fine plan for a hotel, baker, but David wants more than that. He says, "Let me dwell in Your tent forever…" Forever is a lot longer than one night, and he asks for it right out loud.
I see the thinking, baker, since David does mention an enemy. But the verse doesn't put any end date on it. David asks, "Let me dwell in Your tent forever…" There's no "until" in there at all.

True, baker. The very next verse says, "For You have heard my vows, O God…" David asks to dwell in the tent forever, then he says God has heard his vows. He's praying with something behind him, not just hoping.

That one is true, friend, so we'll take the lesson and move on. Right after asking to dwell in God's tent forever, David says, "For You have heard my vows, O God…" That's exactly what the psalm says. David asks, and then he says God has heard.

explanations.answer: He counts himself among those who fear God
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David says God has given him "…the inheritance reserved for those who fear Your name." He places himself in that group. I think that's a humble spot to stand: he's one of the ones who fear God, not a special case.

explanations.answer: He earned it by winning every battle
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The psalm never talks about battles won, and it never says David earned anything. It says God gave him "…the inheritance reserved for those who fear Your name." A gift is a gift, and nobody gets a gift by keeping score.

explanations.answer: He was born into it as Jesse's son
explanations.explanation: Family isn't what the verse points to, baker. David says God gave him "…the inheritance reserved for those who fear Your name." The group in the verse is described by fearing God's name, not by who your father is. Family tree doesn't make the list here.

explanations.answer: Increase the days of his life
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The prayer says, "Increase the days of the king’s life…" Then it keeps going with "may his years span many generations." That's a prayer for a LONG life, and I'd sign up for that one with my mustache.
Edom isn't in this psalm, baker. The prayer for the king says, "Increase the days of the king’s life…" It's about his life stretching out, not a battle report.
Gold is a nice thing to ask for, friend, but it's not in this prayer. The psalm says, "Increase the days of the king’s life…" What it asks for is more days, and you can't stack those in a vault.

Close, baker, but this one is false. The psalm says, "May he sit enthroned in God’s presence forever…" There's no set number of years in it. The word is forever, and that's a different thing than a counted-out term.
Correct, baker. The text says, "May he sit enthroned in God’s presence forever…" No set number of years, just forever. Nobody's counting on a calendar here.

That's it, baker. The prayer says, "appoint Your loving devotion and Your faithfulness to guard him." Think of those two as guards standing watch over the king. I'd take that security detail over the back of a dusty junk drawer any day.

Wisdom and knowledge are great things, friend, but they're not the ones named here. The prayer asks God to "appoint Your loving devotion and Your faithfulness to guard him." Those two are the guards on duty in this verse.

Power and justice sound like strong guards, baker, but they aren't the ones the psalm picks. It says, "appoint Your loving devotion and Your faithfulness to guard him." Devotion and faithfulness are the ones on the job.

explanations.answer: Sing praise and fulfill his vows
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David says, "Then I will ever sing praise to Your name and fulfill my vows day by day." Notice the "…day by day." part. A promise like that isn't kept in one big moment, it's kept one ordinary day after another.

Walls are a big project, baker, but that's not in this psalm. David's closing words are, "Then I will ever sing praise to Your name and fulfill my vows day by day." His plan is to sing and keep his vows, one day at a time.

explanations.answer: Lead the army out to battle
explanations.explanation: The psalm does mention an enemy, friend, but David doesn't close with a battle plan. He says, "Then I will ever sing praise to Your name and fulfill my vows day by day." He ends with singing and keeping his word.
